title: Matter takes the qualities God wills
source_text: Ὅρα οὖν εἰ δεῖ τῷ μετὰ τοιούτων δογμάτων κατηγοροῦντι Χριστιανῶν προσθέσθαι καταλείποντα λόγον, διαφορὰν διδόντα διὰ τὰς ἐπικειμένας ποιότητας τοῖς σώμασι καὶ περὶ τὰ σώματα. ἴσμεν γὰρ καὶ ἡμεῖς ὅτι ἐστὶ „καὶ σώματα ἐπουράνια καὶ σώματα ἐπίγεια,“ καὶ ἄλλη μὲν „ἐπουρανίων“ σωμάτων „δόξα“ ἄλλη δὲ „ἐπιγείων,“ καὶ οὐδὲ τῶν „ἐπουρανίων“ ἡ αὐτή· „ἄλλη“ γὰρ „δόξα ἡλίου“ „καὶ ἄλλη δόξα ἀστέρων,“ καὶ ἐν αὐτοῖς δὲ τοῖς ἄστροις „ἀστὴρ ἀστέρος διαφέρει ἐν δόξῃ.“ διὸ καὶ τὴν ἀνάστασιν „τῶν νεκρῶν“ ἀποδεχόμενοι μεταβολάς φαμεν γίνεσθαι ποιοτήτων τῶν ἐν σώμασιν· ἐπεὶ σπειρόμενά τινα αὐτῶν „ἐν φθορᾷ ἐγείρεται ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ,“ καὶ σπειρόμενα „ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ ἐγείρεται ἐν δόξῃ,“ καὶ σπειρόμενα „ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ ἐγείρεται ἐν δυνάμει,“ καὶ σπειρόμενα σώματα ψυχικὰ ἐγείρεται πνευματικά. περὶ δὲ τοῦ τὴν ὑποκειμένην ὕλην δεκτικὴν εἶναι ποιοτήτων, ὧν ὁ δημιουργὸς βούλεται, πάντες οἱ πρόνοιαν παραδεξάμενοι κατασκευάζομεν· καὶ βουλομένου μὲν θεοῦ ποιότης τοιαδὶ νῦν ἐστι περὶ τήνδε τὴν ὕλην ἑξῆς δὲ τοιαδὶ, φέρ᾿ εἰπεῖν, βελτίων καὶ διαφέρουσα. ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ ὁδοί εἰσι τεταγμέναι τῶν ἐν σώμασι μεταβολῶν, ἐξ οὗ κόσμος ἐστὶ καὶ ἐς ὅσον ἐστὶν, οὐκ οἶδα εἰ καινῆς διαδεξαμένης ὁδοῦ καὶ ἀλλοίας μετὰ τὴν τοῦ κόσμου φθορὰν, καὶ ἣν οἱ ἡμέτεροι λόγοι ὀνομάζουσι συντέλειαν, οὐ θαυμαστὸν εἰ ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος ἐξ ἀνθρώπου νεκροῦ μεταπλασσόμενος ὄφις, ὡς οἱ πολλοί φασι, γίνεται ἀπὸ τοῦ νωτιαίου μυελοῦ καὶ ἐκ βοὸς μέλισσα καὶ ἐξ ἵππου σφὴξ καὶ ἐξ ὄνου κάνθαρος καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς ἐκ τῶν πλείστων σκώληκες. οἴεται δὲ τοῦτο ὁ Κέλσος κατασκευαστικὸν εἶναι τοῦ μηδὲν τούτων ἔργον εἶναι θεοῦ, ἀλλὰ τὰς ποιότητας, οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὁπόθεν οὕτω τεταγμένας ἐκ τῶνδε τάσδε γίνεσθαι, οὐχὶ θείου τινὸς λόγου ἔργον εἶναι, τὰς ἐν τῇ ὕλῃ ποιότητας ἀμείβοντος.
pass_a_gloss: See (ὁράω) then whether one must side with (προστίθημι mid.) the one accusing (κατηγορέω) Christians with such doctrines, abandoning (καταλείπω) an argument (λόγος) that grants difference (διαφορά) because of the qualities (ποιότης) lying upon (ἐπίκειμαι) bodies and about bodies. For we too know that there are 'both heavenly bodies (σώματα ἐπουράνια) and earthly bodies (ἐπίγεια)', and one 'glory' (δόξα) of 'heavenly' bodies, another of 'earthly', and not even of the 'heavenly' the same; for 'other is the glory of the sun and other the glory of stars', and in the stars themselves 'star differs from star in glory'. Therefore also accepting (ἀποδέχομαι) the resurrection (ἀνάστασις) 'of the dead', we say changes (μεταβολή) of qualities in bodies come about; since some of them sown (σπείρω) 'in corruption (φθορά) are raised (ἐγείρω) in incorruption (ἀφθαρσία)', and sown 'in dishonour (ἀτιμία) are raised in glory', and sown 'in weakness (ἀσθένεια) are raised in power (δύναμις)', and bodies sown soul-ish/natural (ψυχικός) are raised spiritual (πνευματικός). About the underlying matter being receptive (δεκτικός) of qualities which the Creator (δημιουργός) wills, all we who have accepted providence (πρόνοια) establish; and God willing, such-and-such quality (ποιότης τοιαδί) is now about this matter, and next such-and-such, let us say, better and differing. And since there are also ordered ways (ὁδοὶ τεταγμέναι) of the changes in bodies, from when the world is and for as long as it is — I do not know whether a new (καινός) and different (ἀλλοῖος) way succeeding (διαδέχομαι) after the destruction (φθορά) of the world, which our writings (οἱ ἡμέτεροι λόγοι) name consummation (συντέλεια) — it is not wonderful if at present from a dead man a serpent (ὄφις) being remoulded (μεταπλάσσω), as the many say, comes from the spinal marrow (νωτιαῖος μυελός), and from an ox a bee (μέλισσα), from a horse a wasp (σφήξ), from an ass a beetle (κάνθαρος), and in short from most things worms (σκώληξ). Celsus thinks this to be probative (κατασκευαστικός) of none of these being God's work, but the qualities, ordered from I know not where so that these come from those, not being the work of some divine reason (θεῖος λόγος) changing (ἀμείβω) the qualities in matter.
pass_b_english: See, then, whether we should side with a man who brings such doctrines to his accusation of Christians, and abandon the argument that allows a difference among bodies because of the qualities laid upon bodies and found in them. For we too know that there are “both heavenly bodies and earthly bodies,” and that the “glory” of “heavenly” bodies is one thing and that of “earthly” bodies another (1 Corinthians 15:40); nor is it the same even among the “heavenly” ones, for “the glory of the sun is one thing, and the glory of the stars another,” and among the stars themselves “star differs from star in glory” (1 Corinthians 15:41). That is why, since we accept the resurrection “of the dead,” we say that changes take place in the qualities that are in bodies. For some of them, sown “in corruption, are raised in incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:42); sown “in dishonour, are raised in glory”; and sown “in weakness, are raised in power” (1 Corinthians 15:43); and bodies sown natural are raised spiritual (1 Corinthians 15:44).

All of us who have accepted providence establish that the underlying matter can receive whatever qualities the Creator wills. By God’s will there is now such-and-such a quality in this matter, and afterwards another, let us say, better and different. There are also fixed courses for the changes in bodies, from the time the world has existed and for as long as it exists — whether a new and different course will take their place after the destruction of the world, which our writings call the consummation (Matthew 24:3), I do not know. Since that is so, it is no wonder if at present, as most people say, a serpent arises from a dead man, reshaped out of his spinal marrow, and a bee from an ox, a wasp from a horse, a beetle from an ass, and, in short, worms from most things. Celsus thinks this proves that none of these is a work of God, and that the qualities, ordered from I know not where so that these arise from those, are not the work of some divine reason that changes the qualities in matter.

choices.choice: nested parenthesis replaced by a dash aside; sentence split so 'since' still governs 'it is no wonder'
μεταπλασσόμενος: 'reshaped out of his spinal marrow'
οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὁπόθεν now modifies τεταγμένας ('ordered from I know not where'), not 'arise'

1 Corinthians 15:40–44 is quoted in fragments, as the quotation marks of the edition show. In 15:41 Origen leaves out Paul's 'and another glory of the moon'. 'Bodies sown natural are raised spiritual' carries no quotation marks in the edition; it closely restates 1 Corinthians 15:44 (σπείρεται σῶμα ψυχικόν, ἐγείρεται σῶμα πνευματικόν) and is cited without quotation marks. ψυχικός is rendered 'natural'. συντέλεια ('consummation') is the Gospel term for the end of the age (Matthew 13:39–40; 24:3; 28:20); cited inline at Matthew 24:3 as the source of the term, not as a quotation. οἱ ἡμέτεροι λόγοι is rendered 'our writings'. The genitive absolute οὐκ οἶδα εἰ καινῆς διαδεξαμένης ὁδοῦ … is taken as Origen's aside and set in parentheses. The beliefs about spontaneous generation (a serpent from a corpse's spinal marrow, bees from an ox, wasps from a horse, beetles from an ass) are reported 'as most people say'; their classical sources are not cited because Origen names none. θείου τινὸς λόγου is indefinite and left lowercase ('some divine reason').
